extracted.intended_audience: general public and podcast listeners interested in environmental investigative journalism (Deepwater Horizon fallout)
extracted.subtask_description: Transcript and accompanying article for a radio/podcast episode investigating the Deepwater Horizon oil spill's ongoing impacts, combining interviews, archival material, expert analysis, and reporting. Meant to inform and engage listeners/readers about human, regulatory, and environmental consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek comment from implicated parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporter contacts involved organizations for their response (e.g., 'I reached out to BP for a comment about these lawsuits ... BP responded that the company does not comment on active litigation').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show attempts to get the subject's perspective, include their response verbatim or summarize if they decline, and note when an organization refuses to comment or limits comment due to litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include multiple perspectives and sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a range of voices — affected people, investigative reporters, regulators, and subject-matter experts (examples in the episode: Sara Sneath, Sheree Kerner, Kevin Sligh, Donald Boesch).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance first-person testimony with reporting and expert analysis to provide context and corroboration; explicitly identify interviewees and their roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose production, funding, and contact information
rubrics_metrics.description: List production credits and funding/support (e.g., 'Produced and hosted by Carlyle Calhoun and Sara Sneath'; 'Sea Change is made possible with major support from the Gulf Research Program of the National Academy of Sciences...'); provide author contact ('You can reach her at: carlyle@wwno.org').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make production team and funders transparent; include contact info for the host/producer so readers can follow up or provide tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use archival materials and direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate archival audio/quotes and historical statements to contextualize events (e.g., archival presidential and CEO quotes, archival headlines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Label archival material clearly, provide verbatim quotes when available, and use archival content to show historical framing or contrast with current reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present factual data and quantitative estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Include concrete figures and scientific estimates about impacts (examples: '87 days', 'more than 200 million gallons of oil', '167,000 sea turtles', 'more than 33,000 people worked to clean up').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide numeric data and, where possible, attribute to studies, scientists, or official estimates; use figures to quantify scale and impact while indicating the source or uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full transcript and subscription/access info
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a written transcript of the episode and prominent ways to subscribe (shown as 'TRANSCRIPT' and 'Ways To Subscribe: Apple, Spotify, Stitcher, Pandora, Amazon Music').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improve accessibility and discoverability by publishing a transcript and listing subscription platforms; transcripts also support verification and quoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use investigative documents and evidentiary reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Support reporting with obtained documents and internal communications when possible (example: 'we found some documents that BP's executives were talking amongst each other...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite or describe documentary evidence that corroborates reporting, explain how documents were obtained, and use them to substantiate claims about corporate knowledge or conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center personal testimonies to humanize systemic issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature detailed personal accounts from affected individuals to illustrate human consequences (e.g., Sheree Kerner's account of her husband Frank Stuart's illness and death).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person narratives to connect readers emotionally to the issue, but corroborate with data and expert analysis to avoid anecdotal overreach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose potential conflicts of interest or funder relationships relevant to coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Make explicit any relationships that might bear on coverage (example: 'a recent report released by the National Academy of Sciences, who I should note is a funder of Sea Change').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State funders or institutional relationships that are connected to sources or coverage to maintain transparency and allow readers to judge potential biases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attribute and distinguish opinions, analysis, and factual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearly label expert judgments, host commentary, and factual claims (the episode frames expert quotes and the host's framing separately, e.g., 'Donald said...'; host commentary follows).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep factual reporting distinct from interpretation or opinion by attributing claims to sources and signaling when a statement is analysis or conjecture.
